item.title: The Hague’s historic jenever distillery is fighting for its life
item.description:
The Hague’s historic jenever distillery is fighting for its life

September 6, 2026 Brandon Hartley

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The iconic Van Kleef Distillery dates back to 1776. It’s faced countless challenges since then, but the latest round could force it to close or substantially change.

For over two centuries, the Van Kleef Distillery in The Hague has been mixing up unique liqueurs and genever made with time-tested recipes. Vincent van Gogh is one of the customers known to have sampled its spirits.

Despite its rich history and status as the last remaining distillery in the city, owner Fleur Kruyt says Van Kleef is currently facing a series of setbacks that could shut down its long-time location on the Lange Beestenmarkt.

“Right now I have the same colour hair as my grandmother at the age of 96,” she told DutchNews during an interview in the distillery’ tasting room.

Kruyt has spent the past several years trying to come up with solutions to appease her landlord and city officials as she strives to expand Van Kleef’s operations, modernise its museum, and, more than anything else, prevent its doors from closing altogether.

It’s all enough to turn the hair of even the most steadfast and indomitable of small business owners completely white.

But these challenges are only the latest in Van Kleef’s tumultuous history. Over the years, it’s contended with the sudden death of an owner, a crime wave, overzealous safety inspectors, and the Covid pandemic.

The first few centuries
The distillery dates all the way back to the late 18th century. It originally opened in 1776 as Distilleerderij “Anker” before being taken over by the Van Kleef family in 1842.

Kruyt is convinced Van Gogh stopped by at least once. The famous artist may have even been a regular given his proclivities. He lived down the street from 1869 to 1873 and spent those years working at Goupil & Cie, an art business in The Hague owned by his uncle.

Along with the rest of the Netherlands, the distillery managed to endure the impacts of the Spanish flu pandemic and two World Wars, but it was a safety inspection in 1986 that came much closer to shutting it down.

Explosive concerns
The officials declared the 40,000 litres of alcohol sitting in the distillery’s vats were a huge safety risk that made it an almost literal ticking time bomb. They decided it was no longer safe to distill alcohol on the property.

At the time, Van Kleef was teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. The surrounding neighbourhood was considered a “no-go zone” for many of the city’s residents and the distillery wasn’t getting much foot traffic.

“If you walked these streets as a woman at night back then, you were either a prostitute or tired of your life,” Kruyt said. “There was lots of criminality. No one came here anymore.”

After much discussion and planning, production was moved off site. The building itself was purchased by a local development company called Stadsherstel Den Haag and Van Kleef officially became a tenant in its long-time home.

The books were eventually balanced after it attained historical status and Van Kleef finally reopened as a multipurpose operation in 1995. Along with the museum and a tasting room, Van Kleef’s liqueurs are bottled and labelled there to this day.

Even more setbacks
The construction of a tram tunnel and the redesign of the street out front dragged on for over a decade and further drove customers away.

The distillery’s revenue dropped by 80% when the city began installing barriers around the neighbourhood to discourage auto traffic in 2009. Its suppliers and customers had to navigate a maze every time they tried to go there.

Kruyt, who was operating Van Kleef with her husband Louis Centazzo at the time, was forced to use their house as collateral on a loan to keep it open. Then he suddenly died in 2015, leaving her to manage the distillery on her own.

Foreclosure followed and Kruyt moved into an apartment on the property. The hits kept coming as gentrification quickly transformed the neighbourhood and raised the distillery’s monthly rent along with it.

Then the Covid crisis began, which forced Van Kleef to shut down its tasting room. Undaunted, Kruyt and her crew came up with clever ways to ensure revenue would keep coming in.

She joked that “booze was declared a necessity” during the pandemic. Kruyt developed a “vaccine” after inspiration struck while she was giving her dog injections for arthritis. “The Van Kleef Vaccine” is a mix of Limoncello, Vitamin C, and ginger-infused liqueur.

At first, Kruyt fretted that it wouldn’t go over well with customers who had spent weeks social distancing and worrying they’d be the next ones to catch Covid. Those fears proved unfounded.

“And the first people who bought it? Doctors and pharmacists,” she recalled. “They found it really cool. I thought, ‘If these people find it funny, I don’t care about the rest!’”

A “ginitiser” sold in spray bottles soon followed. It, too, was a hit.

The current dilemmas
“We’ve always managed and, whenever I feel bad, I turn on the television and see how it could be a lot worse,” Kruyt said before discussing the latest round of threats to the distillery.

The city’s decision to impose a flat €50-a-day parking fee has taken another bite out of Van Kleef’s revenue. The policy was so controversial it was even covered by The Guardian in 2023. If all this wasn’t enough, Kruyt broke her ankle while on a summer holiday and the recovery process required several surgeries.

Determined to keep the distillery where it’s been for over 200 years, Kruyt has been combating another wave of financial woes coupled with bureaucratic headaches, soaring energy bills, and other increased costs. Even the price of the glass that goes into Van Kleef’s bottles has gone up recently.

A crowdfunding campaign has been underway since 2025. Plans were also made to expand operations to attract more visitors, but negotiations with Stadsherstel Den Haag have proven challenging.

After over two years of discussions about everything from the future of the museum to renovations for the apartments on the property, Kruyt said the situation has been handed over to a new director named Jan-Willem de Bruijn.

“Stadsherstel Den Haag is currently taking a comprehensive look at the complex,” De Bruijn told DutchNews. “This means that, in addition to the shop and the tasting room, we are also focusing on the redevelopment of the museum and garden as well as upgrades in the apartments. In doing so, we aim to invest sustainably in the preservation of this unique and characteristic part of The Hague.”

Delays with permitting haven’t helped. DutchNews contacted the office of Alderwoman Saskia Bruines for comment about this and other matters concerning the distillery, but had not received a response as of press time.

Fighting onward
Regardless of what happens next, Kruyt says Van Kleef will continue in one form or another, even if that means turning it into a distillery-and-wholesaler-only operation at a facility closed to the public and likely located on the outskirts of The Hague.

“But all of this history would go away,” she said as she gestured towards the centuries-old equipment in Van Kleef’s museum.

Takeaway liqueurs and tastings have covered the costs of maintaining the distillery’s historical inventory, but the current circumstances have made that impossible to continue. As Kruyt faces another round of discussions with Stadsherstel Den Haag, she’s determined to stay optimistic.

“We met with Jan-Willem a few weeks ago,” she said. “We’re really happy that he is taking everything seriously and trying to preserve the heritage that we have here.”

Still open for business
Visitors to Van Kleef can currently visit the small museum, enjoy drinks and snacks in its tasting room, host gatherings in a former storage cellar turned conference room, and purchase bottles of liqueurs made with recipes that date back to the 17th century.

Among them is Bridal Tears, which contains flakes of 24-carat gold. It was once a popular wedding gift. The bawdy tales and traditions surrounding it and two accompanying liqueurs could fill an entire book.

In an age of alcoholic beverages with preservatives and other ingredients that are difficult to describe, let alone pronounce the names of, Van Kleef is still doing things the old-fashioned way.

“All of our recipes have been preserved,” Kruyt said. “We have an archive full of them that began in the 1840s. Everything you’re tasting is real in the sense that there’s no artificial flavouring or colourings.”

The distillery continues to attract international visitors and aficionados of liqueurs. Kruyt said a few of them are household names, but she demurred when asked for the details.

“What happens at Van Kleef, stays at Van Kleef,” she said. “So any celebrities out there, you can come here and we won’t talk about you.”

item.title: The Many Lives of Anne Frank: a fascinating work
item.description:
The Many Lives of Anne Frank: a fascinating work

September 5, 2026 Molly Quell

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Many Lives of Anne Frank is a biography, of the German Jewish teenager herself, of her famous diary and, also, of her legacy. Ruth Franklin’s innovative approach to the most famous work of the Holocaust is fascinating, thought-provoking and well worth the read.

The Diary of Anne Frank has been assigned to thousands of students and has sold millions of copies. The annex where the teenager hid with her family during the Second World War is visited by a million tourists a year, whose queue snakes along the canal in Amsterdam for blocks.

Published in 2025, the first half of the book is a classic biography. We follow the Frank family from Germany to exile in the Netherlands and then to further banishment above a warehouse on the Prinsengracht. Franklin brings the story to life, with minute details (it was raining on the evening the Franks walked across the Dutch capital to their hiding place) and wider context (the ongoing round-up of Jews by the occupying Nazis.)

The biography does not end, as most biographies do, with the subject’s death. The young girl died somewhere in March or April of 1945 at Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, possibly just weeks before it was liberated by the British army.

Her legacy lives on, in her diary published, following edits from her father, shortly after the war. Anne herself also edited the work, inspired by a 1944 appeal from the Dutch minister for education diaries and letters documenting the German occupation. The teen aspired to get her thoughts and feelings into print.

The second half of the book follows the legacy of the diary, how it came into being and how it became a phenomenon, vaulting Anne Frank to an epic level of fame.

Franklin delves into the details of the book’s publication journey, raising questions about what it means for something to be “authentic.”

Anne’s father Otto sends a translated (and edited) version to relatives in Switzerland, who encourage him to publish the work. A composite of Anne’s two versions, plus her father’s edits is submitted to a publisher, who suggests certain cuts as to not offend more conservative readers. A longer, critical edition was published in 1986 and, based on that, the English-language version was published in 1989.

The first German-language version edits a passage Anne wrote taking a dig at the country. She writes “Only civilized languages are permitted [in the Annex], therefore no German,” which is changed to “all civilised languages may be spoken.” The occupants made an effort to speak to one another in Dutch, rather than in their native German, as a form of resistance.

The chapters are all titled with descriptors of the various versions of Anne. The final one is called “Pawn” and addresses her legacy. Otto intended for the diary to “promote peace and tolerance,” Franklin writes, but he couldn’t control his daughter’s celebrity.

The adaptation of the diary in a play in the United States is complicated by differing artistic versions of the work, the iconic image of Anne is used by those protesting South African apartheid and later, Israel’s war on Gaza. Franklin’s chronicle leaves the reader with many questions about how to contextualise the diary of a teenage girl.

A prize-winning literary critic, Franklin is a former editor at The New Republic. Her first biography, Shirley Jackson: A Rather Haunted Life, won multiple awards. The Many Lives of Anne Frank was a finalist for the 2025 Los Angeles Times Book Prizes.

The Many Lives of Anne Frank is deeply researched, well-written and stimulating.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

item.title: Amsterdam travel app leaked users’ personal data for months
item.description:
Amsterdam travel app leaked users’ personal data for months

September 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Polarsteps, an Amsterdam-founded travel app used by more than 23 million people, left users’ photos, locations and home addresses reachable by anyone through an unsecured data feed – including trips put on private mode – and had known about the flaw for months, an investigation by Follow the Money (FTM) has found.

The investigation found that anyone could connect to the free app’s data feed and pull users’ names, 230 million photos and videos, and 1 billion GPS locations from nearly 2 million trips – enough to plot journeys on a map and follow many of them close to real time.

More than a million of those trips had been shared only with followers. Even accounts set fully to private gave away who a user followed, who followed them and which device they logged in from. And once FTM held the link to someone’s trip, removing it as a follower changed nothing.

Home addresses were among the most sensitive details exposed. FTM pinned down dozens from the exact location saved inside users’ photos – a shot of packed suitcases taken at home, for example, and worked out many more from the spots people returned to each night.

That photo-location data appeared nowhere in Polarsteps’ privacy policy, and was missing from the file the company released when FTM asked to see its own records.

A year’s warning
The problem was first flagged last year by a French cybersecurity researcher who said Polarsteps told him it already knew what was happening. He took his findings to FTM, which said the data stayed exposed for at least six months.

Marc Schuilenburg, a professor of digital surveillance at Erasmus University, called the company negligent, and warned that leaked location data can be used to stalk, harass or threaten people.

The leak was not from a hack – no passwords were taken and no accounts entered. Anyone with basic technical skill could connect to Polarsteps’ servers and scrape the data, with none of the request limits, CAPTCHAs or login walls.

Company response
Polarsteps, which has grown from 1 million users in 2019, said no passwords or accounts were compromised and that it is in contact with the AP.

Chief executive Clare Jones, appointed in 2024, said the company should have caught the problem itself and was working out what went wrong. It has since tightened its systems, and noted that much of the exposed data had been made public by users’ own choice.

The company’s own website warns travellers that sharing location details in real time “can make you a target.” FTM said a second part of its investigation, on dozens of military personnel it tracked to bases and missions at home and abroad, would follow on Saturday.

item.title: Prosecutors hold 32 over Overasselt attack, including two minors
item.description:
Prosecutors hold 32 over Overasselt attack, including two minors

September 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Public prosecutors are detaining 32 people on suspicion of murder or manslaughter in connection with the killing of a security guard in Overasselt on Tuesday.

Thirty-four people were initially arrested in the area surrounding the Gelderland village but two were released as there was insufficient evidence to hold them. CCTV footage shows dozens of masked men getting out of a truck outside the property, some heavily armed, before one shoots a man sitting in a car.

They also opened fire on police shortly afterwards, injuring two. Of those arrested, two are minors aged 16 and 17, the rest are men from France, Netherlands, Algeria, Libya, Belgium and Ukraine – all aged between 18 and 32.

Footage emerged online after the attack purportedly by a drugs gang, threatening the resident of the property that was attacked and saying that he had stolen a large quantity of goods from them.

That man, known as Jan G. Jr, has been barred from entering the council around Overasselt for at least two weeks and will not be allowed back to live in the property for at least a year.

He has been linked to the drugs trade before and the house was shot at last year with an AK-47 by a young man from Amsterdam, said to be a drug addict who was paid to carry out the attack. He never named who paid him.

item.title: Public officials among those abusing Jetten online, AD finds
item.description:
Public officials among those abusing Jetten online, AD finds

September 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A council official, a police employee and a member of the Dutch air force are among thousands of people posting homophobic abuse under prime minister Rob Jetten’s social media messages on X, an investigation by the Algemeen Dagblad (AD) has found.

The paper analysed 45,860 replies to 323 posts sent from the prime minister’s official account during his first six months in office. One in 20 – 2,293 replies – was homophobic, it said.

The abuse appeared under routine posts, from a congratulatory message for Queen Máxima to a post about Amsterdam Pride, and did not depend on the topics Jetten was writing about.

AD identified two recurring forms of abuse. The first was crude slurs and the second, far more common, was a single insinuating question posted in Dutch hundreds of times: “Did you tell them you’re gay?”

Hard to prosecute
Most of the accounts did not belong to anonymous trolls, AD said. The large majority left a single homophobic reply and never returned, and the 10 most persistent accounts together produced less than 6% of the total.

Only a handful of repeat posters could be traced, among them the council, police and air force employees. Marloes van Noorloos, a professor of criminal law at Leiden University, told the paper that the insinuating questions were hard to prosecute as hate speech or criminal insult, because it depends largely on wording and context.

Civil servants, she said, could face disciplinary action under the rules governing public employees.

Jetten’s response
Jetten is the Netherlands’ first openly gay prime minister, and has said he files a police report every week over the abuse he receives about his sexuality. At the WorldPride conference last month he said big social media companies were “barely moderating content for hate speech”.

X’s own rules prohibit attacking users over their sexual orientation, but the company has taken little action, according to AD.

Dutch acceptance of homosexuality has stalled after years of progress. Jetten has said the Netherlands needs to get back on track and return to the top 10 countries for LGBTQI+ rights, from where it fell to number 13 after 2018.

item.title: Farmers face livestock cuts as nitrogen plan falls short
item.description:
Farmers face livestock cuts as nitrogen plan falls short

September 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch farmers are still facing a compulsory cut in the number of animals they can keep as livestock, after the government’s environmental assessment agency found the cabinet’s nitrogen plan would fall just short of its own 2035 target.

The agency, PBL, assessed the €20 billion nitrogen plan at the cabinet’s request and called it an important step that could bring the farming emissions target within reach.

But it found the measures worked out so far leave a gap, and that an across-the-board cut of 5% to 10% in farmers’ livestock rights, the permits that cap how many animals a farm may hold, is still needed.

The coalition has always said that a blanket cut is a last resort, to be used only if the targets are missed in 2035. Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen called it an “emergency brake” on Friday and “a no-go for the cabinet.”

Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, against 2019 levels, under the package agreed in June. PBL expects the herd to shrink further regardless as farms adapt to those rules, with some businesses forced to close.

The agency was more positive about the plan’s benefits for the environment, but warned the nitrogen problem will not just disappear. On more than half the area of the most sensitive protected sites, deposition is still expected to breach the critical threshold in 2035.

Nature groups called the plans the minimum needed to start repairing decades of damage. The farmers’ party BBB and the farm lobby LTO said the extra cut was unacceptable, though LTO is staying at the table to negotiate the rest of the package.

item.title: Dutch soil scientist wins Ig Nobel for burying 1,000 underpants
item.description:
Dutch soil scientist wins Ig Nobel for burying 1,000 underpants

September 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Dutch scientist has won the Ig Nobel prize for conducting a study that involved burying around 1,000 pairs of underpants and digging them up two months later.

Marcel van der Heijden, a soil scientist at the University of Zurich, shared this year’s Ig Nobel for soil science with three colleagues. The annual prizes, a parody counterpart to the Nobels, reward research that “first makes people laugh and then makes them think.”

Volunteers buried identical cotton underpants across more than 25 countries, then dug them up after two months and recorded what was left. The more the fabric had rotted, the healthier and more biologically active the soil.

“Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” van der Heijden said in a statement, adding that healthy soil was crucial for fertility and for the wider ecosystem.

This year’s ceremony was held in Zurich, the first time it has taken place outside the US after more than three decades in the country.

Organisers said they could not in good conscience ask winners or visiting journalists to travel to the US this year, a decision widely assumed to be down to American immigration policy. Next year’s event will be in Antwerp.

Dutch researchers are Ig Nobel regulars. According to broadcaster NOS, they have won 22 times since the first ceremony in 1991, including last year’s award for showing that a drink can improve people’s foreign-language skills.

item.title: Dutch road traffic CO2 falls for first time since pandemic
item.description:
Dutch road traffic CO2 falls for first time since pandemic

September 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Emissions from road traffic in the Netherlands fell in 2025 for the first time since the Covid pandemic, according to figures from the national statistics agency CBS.

Vehicles produced 26.6 million tonnes of CO2 last year, 1.6% less than in 2024 and 2.2% below the level of a decade earlier.

Passenger cars account for almost 58% of the total. Their emissions fell 1.9% on the year even though the distance driven rose slightly. Fully electric cars produce no CO2 while being driven, and around 7.4% of cars on the road were fully electric in 2025.

The saving covers tailpipe emissions only, not the CO2 released to generate the electricity used to charge those cars.

Emissions from vans and lorries, which together make up 40% of the road total, also fell, mainly because commercial vehicles were driven fewer kilometres.

The longer-term picture is more mixed. While car emissions were 9.1% lower than in 2015, those from vans and lorries were higher, as the distance driven by commercial vehicles rose over the decade.

The Netherlands remains well short of its climate law target of a 55% cut in greenhouse gas emissions on 1990 levels by 2030.

item.title: Rents rise 4.4% nationally, Rotterdam hit hardest
item.description:
Rents rise 4.4% nationally, Rotterdam hit hardest

September 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Rents in the Netherlands rose by an average of 4.4% in July compared with a year earlier, national statistics office CBS has reported, a slower increase than in either of the past two years.

The rise was lower than the 4.9% recorded in 2025 and the 5.4% in 2024, then the steepest increase in more than 30 years. Most landlords in the Netherlands raise rents once a year, in July.

The average covers two different things. Tenants who stayed where they were saw a 3.8% rise but rents rose faster when a new tenant moved in.

Where rents rose most
Among the four big cities, rents rose most in Rotterdam, at 4.7%, and least in Amsterdam, at 4.3%. The Hague saw 4.4% and the city of Utrecht 4.5%. By province, the steepest rises were in Overijssel and Noord-Brabant, both at 4.6%, and the smallest in Friesland, at 4%.

The government sets annual caps on rents for each part of the market, at 4.1% for social housing this year. Rents can still rise above the cap when a home is re-let, or when higher earners are charged an extra €50 or €100 a month.

For private-sector tenants, housing already takes a bigger share of income than for any other group, up to 35% for those entering the market, CBS reported earlier this year.
